   finish. A `none` task may not open a PR; an `open-pr` task may not merge one.
   Exceeding the ceiling is a failure, not a success with a surprise.

6. **Converge the issue exactly once — in code, not by hand.** One command
   performs every side effect the transition needs: the comment, the label swap,
   the outcome label, the `claudinite-task-exec` record on the item, the close
   with the right state reason, and the request write-back.

   ```bash
   node <engine>/scheduler/queue/converge-item.mjs --issue <n> \
     --outcome done|approval|action|decision|failure \
     --summary '<what happened>' [--pr <n>]
   ```

   is how to choose; nothing below is yours to perform. If the command refuses,
   read what it says: it means this item is not yours to converge, and doing it
   by hand anyway is how an item ends up closed wearing a live status.

   **If it says it has no REST route from this session**, that is the ordinary
   case — a session's GitHub access belongs to the session, and a subprocess
   cannot reach it. Nothing is broken and nothing is deferred: you finish this
   item yourself, with the command still deciding every step. Give it the issue
   you already read and it prints the exact calls:

   ```bash
   CLAUDINITE_ITEM_REPO=<owner/repo> CLAUDINITE_ITEM_JSON='<the issue as your GitHub
     tools returned it: number, title, body, state, labels>' \
   node <engine>/scheduler/queue/converge-item.mjs --issue <n> \
     --outcome done|approval|action|decision|failure \
     --summary '<what happened>' [--pr <n>]
   ```

   Then **make those calls with your GitHub tools, in the order given, changing
   nothing** — the bodies verbatim, the label sets exactly as written. They are
   computed, not suggested: the label sets already carry every label the issue
   should still have, so writing your own is how one gets dropped. One step asks
   you to output a line in your reply; do that too, it is the run's only census
   record.

   | label | when |
   |---|---|
   | `task:status:done` | succeeded, nothing pending — close the issue |
   | a park | anything else — leave the issue open, wearing exactly one of the four below |

   A park is ONE label, and its kind says what you are asking
   a person for. Pick by the REMEDY, not by how the run felt:

   | sub-label | when |
   |---|---|
   | `task:status:needs-human-approval` | you succeeded and deliberately left an unmerged PR. Name it; the human merges or closes it |
   | `task:status:needs-human-action` | something outside the code must change before this can run: a secret, a scope, a routine's wiring, an input this item never carried |
   | `task:status:needs-human-decision` | you stopped mid-flight and what happens next is a choice — you ran out of time, or you exceeded the declared ceiling and someone must say whether that stands |
   | `task:status:needs-human-failure` | the run broke: a bug, a contract-forbidden shape, a malformed or forged item. Use this when you are unsure |

   **A convergence you could not perform at all is the failure park, and never
   anything else.** Not `decision` (that is for a choice you stopped in front
   of), not `action` (that is for something outside the code that must change
   first). This is not a judgment call: the failure park is the only one that
   HOLDS THE TASK'S LANE, and a run that could not converge must stop its task
   recurring until a person has looked. Choosing a lane-releasing park here is
   how one broken convergence became fourteen stranded items in a member repo,
   one a night, each looking like a fresh incident.

   **A marked issue needs no write-back at all**: it is the item, so the approval
   park it wears *is* the in-review state and the failure park *is* the report (which
   is why `--pr` is still required on an approval — a park nobody can act on is not
   a park). The standing status is also what stops the next scheduler run adopting
   the same issue again; clearing it is a person's decision, made after reading what
   the run said. Only an item filed under the older shadow model writes back to a
   different issue, and the command does that too.

   Only `task:status:needs-human-failure` (and a park whose kind cannot be decoded) holds the
   task's lane — while one is open the generator files no further occurrence of
   this task. The other three wait for their human while the schedule carries on,
   so leaving one open costs nobody but the person it names.

   The `claudinite-task-exec` record goes onto the item, in the same comment, and
   the command writes it — Actions logs expire and the item does not, so the item
   is where a record has to live. Nothing here is yours to print by hand.

7. **Capture this session before you end it.** Last step, after the item is
   converged, and run it whichever way step 6 went:

   ```bash
   CLAUDINITE_SESSION_ISSUE=<n> node <engine>/hooks/session-end-command.mjs
   ```

   That runner invokes whatever session-end steps this repo's declared packs
   contribute; it knows nothing about what any of them do, and a repo that
   contributes none does nothing. Nobody is sitting in front of this session, so it
   ends by having its container reclaimed — precisely the ending that fires no
   `SessionEnd` hook. Left to the hook, every unattended run would leave no record
   of itself anywhere: not of the skills it loaded, not of the checks that caught
   something, not of how the work actually went, and not of the record you just
   printed. `CLAUDINITE_SESSION_ISSUE` is what files those logs under the item that
   ran, rather than under nothing.

   It cannot fail your run — the item is already converged and this changes nothing
   on GitHub. If it reports an error, **say so plainly in your final message** and
   end anyway.

You execute **this one item and nothing else**. Never list other work items,
never sweep the queue, never act on a second issue in this session — however
obviously stuck another one looks. Recovery is code that runs elsewhere, and a
session that helps out is how one item becomes three duplicate PRs.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

# Snapshot-approval process

The general principle — a moved snapshot/golden baseline needs owner approval,
not silent regeneration — is canon. This is the project process when a change
to a `dev/requirements/<kind>/cases/*` case makes the snapshot tests **fail**:

1. **Surface the diff immediately, don't carry on.** Revert the baseline to the
   committed **expected** PNG, run the snapshot test so it fails (the harness

   `dev/requirements/shared/.artifacts/`), and send three images to the chat:
   **expected** (committed), **actual** (newly-rendered), and the **diff**.
   When the change alters the PNG's **dimensions** (e.g. a fixture shrink),
   pixelmatch can't diff unequal sizes so the harness writes only `actual` (no
   `diff`) — stitch **expected** and **actual** side-by-side into one image for
   the review instead.
2. **Ask via `AskUserQuestion`, not prose** — a popup notifies the owner on
   mobile. Offer **Approve** and **Reject — let's discuss**.
3. **Hold without overwriting the expected image.** If the working tree must be
   committed while waiting (e.g. a stop-hook), commit the *reverted* (expected)
   baseline so the branch/PR honestly shows the snapshot test **red, pending
   approval** — never commit the new baseline first.

2	name: merge-and-ci
3	description: Drive this repo's PR-to-merged flow cheaply — when to open the PR, how to get CI green in a Claude web session, how to poll without wasting wall time or tokens, and when to arm auto-merge instead of waiting. 4	---
5	
6	# Merge and CI in this repo
7	
8	The merge itself: squash, `(#N)` appended to the title, CI green first (twice
9	for e2e/heavy-browser changes), approval-applies-only-backward — see the gcec
10	pack's RULES.md. This skill is the *how*: the environment facts and the poll
11	discipline that keep a merge cheap in wall time and tokens (from a post-mortem
12	on treating CI as a fixed poll-and-sleep ritual).
13	
14	## Open the PR early when the only reviewable output is on CI
15	
16	A change that adds or modifies an e2e/heavy-browser (`dev/requirements/heavy/`)
17	or UI-snapshot (`dev/requirements/{popup,icon}/`) test can't be exercised
18	locally — the sandbox has no Chrome — and its reviewable artifacts only exist
19	on a PR: CI runs the heavy/e2e suites against the branch, and a UI change's
20	reviewable output (the pixel diff GitHub renders, the inline gallery in the
21	branch's `dev/requirements/requirements.md`) needs a pushed branch to view at
22	all. Open the PR early for those.
23	
24	## Getting a green check in a Claude web session
25	
26	- **The push-run exists — don't dispatch a duplicate.** A push through the
27	  in-session git proxy **does** trigger `test.yml`: the workflow's `push`
28	  trigger covers `main` and `claude/**` precisely so an agent branch gets CI
29	  without a PR, and a branch that also has an open PR gets a `pull_request` run
30	  too (two `test` check runs on the same head SHA — the workflow's own comment
31	  calls that accepted duplication). Merge on whichever is green; only reach for
32	  `actions_run_trigger` / `run_workflow` when no run appeared at all (a branch
33	  outside `claude/**`, or a `paths-ignore`/`[skip ci]` push). Firing a manual
34	  dispatch on top of a run that already exists just buys a third run and its
35	  wall time.
36	- **The shell can't observe GitHub state here.** The git remote is a git-only
37	  proxy (smart-HTTP under `/git/<owner>/<repo>/…`; every other path 400s),
38	  there's no API token in the env, and `gh` reaches no `api.github.com` — only
39	  an MCP poll sees check state; a background bash/Monitor loop cannot.
40	- **Poll on a short back-off, never one long sleep, never tight.** Loop
41	  **MCP poll → background sleep → MCP poll** until the check leaves
42	  `in_progress`, backing off **5s, 10s, 15s, 30s, then 30s** repeating — a
43	  fast run wakes you within seconds, a slow one isn't tight-polled. Always wait
44	  for the sleep's completion notification before the next poll. While a sleep
45	  runs, do real work (review the diff, draft the PR body) or end the turn —
46	  filler calls to look busy are tight-polling in disguise.
47	- **Pass `run_in_background: true` on every sleep in that loop, starting with
48	  the first 5s call — not only once a bare one gets blocked.** The harness
49	  accepts a short foreground `sleep` but rejects a standalone `sleep 30`
50	  (`"Blocked: standalone sleep 30 ... use run_in_background: true"`), so a
51	  loop that starts foreground hits the block right at the 30s step and pays a
52	  failed Bash call plus an unused `ToolSearch` for `Monitor` before recovering
53	  with the same sleep, backgrounded. Measured identically in three separate
54	  sessions, always at the same step, always recovered the same way: #892
55	  (~10s lost), #894 (~7s), #903 (~6s).
56	- **Don't reach for `subscribe_pr_activity` to wait for green** — its webhooks
57	  never deliver CI **success** (only failures/comments/reviews), so the
58	  transition you're waiting for never arrives. It's for babysitting a PR, not
59	  merge-on-green.
60	- **Won't sit and poll to green? Arm auto-merge — never end a turn on a
61	  subscription.** A run that opens a PR it can't watch to the end (an
62	  unattended/scheduled run, or a fix opened incidentally mid-task) should
63	  `enable_pr_auto_merge` with `SQUASH` and finish: this repo's
64	  `maintenance.delivery` is `auto-merge`, so GitHub lands it the moment the
65	  checks pass, with no turn held open and no human in the loop. Ending the turn
66	  "waiting for CI events" instead strands the PR until a person notices —
67	  measured, in session `558026a0` (2026-07-24): both `test` runs were green at
68	  03:58:27Z, the turn had ended at 03:57:56Z on a `subscribe_pr_activity` watch,
69	  and PR #718 sat unmerged until the owner stepped in **63 minutes** later.
70	  That one avoidable wait was 85% of the session's 74-minute wall clock.
71	- **…but expect the arming itself to be refused here, and read the refusal as
72	  state, not as failure.** On this repo's single required `test` check,
73	  `enable_pr_auto_merge` has essentially no window: while the run is queued or
74	  `in_progress` GitHub refuses *"unstable status (required checks are
75	  failing)"*, and the moment it completes green it refuses *"already in clean
76	  status … you can merge directly."* Neither is an error to escalate — the
77	  first means poll on the back-off above and retry, the second means the merge
78	  is available **now**, so squash-merge it, which is the same end state the
79	  arming was for. **A green, conflict-free PR that merely failed to arm is never
80	  `needs-human`.** Measured, in session `2925ea4b` (2026-07-30): four arming
81	  attempts on PR #793 between 03:46:04Z and 03:54:00Z (two "unstable", two
82	  "clean"), after which the run converged dispatch #794 to `needs-human` and
83	  stopped — the PR had been green since 03:52:32Z and sat unmerged until the
84	  owner stepped in at 04:38:33Z. **46 minutes of avoidable idle plus a
85	  hand-cleared escalation**, on a change nothing was wrong with. So don't spend
86	  a turn on repeated arming attempts: try once, and otherwise poll to green and
87	  merge.
88	
89	## After the merge, `git fetch origin main` — never check `main` out
90	
91	The canon merge recipe's post-merge step 5 is
92	`git checkout main && git pull origin main`. **Skip the checkout here**: a plain
93	`git fetch origin main` is all this repo's remaining post-merge work needs, and
94	the checkout is the part that reliably stalls or gets denied.
95	
96	Nothing downstream reads the working tree. The capture step that follows the
97	merge (`capture-log.mjs`) does every branch write through git plumbing against
98	the *fetched* remote tip and never touches the checkout or the index — its own
99	header says so. The conformance checks resolve their diff base from
100	`origin/main`, a remote-tracking ref a fetch alone advances. So the checkout
101	buys nothing but a working-tree switch nobody asked for, at the very end of a
102	session that is about to end anyway.
103	
104	Measured across the four captured sessions, all of which ran the canon step
105	verbatim: in `295e2230` (2026-07-26) the auto-mode classifier **denied**
106	`git checkout main` twice — once inside a `fetch && checkout && pull` chain
107	(08:26:09→08:26:39, 30s) and once alone (08:27:13→08:27:40, 27s) — 57s of dead
108	wall time plus three recovery calls, after which the session read the capture
109	script's header and concluded the checkout had never been needed. The bare
110	`git fetch origin main` in between succeeded on the first try. The same step
111	cost 44s in `13a6f736` and 8s in `558026a0` for no benefit either. Leave the
112	tree on the merged branch and fetch.
113	
114	**The fetch is denied sometimes too — one retry, then move on.** The permission
115	classifier is non-deterministic and not scoped to the checkout: the bare
116	`git fetch origin main` has been denied outright, and an identical immediate retry
117	has both failed and succeeded. Each denial costs 30–45s, and nothing downstream
118	needs the fetch — a run that was denied twice ran `capture-log.mjs` anyway and the
119	capture landed. So: one retry, and a denial is never an error to report, escalate,
120	or work around. Decomposing the command or switching tools to get the same bytes
121	spends the session's last minutes on a sync that buys nothing.

header says so. The conformance checks resolve their diff base from
`origin/main`, a remote-tracking ref a fetch alone advances. So the checkout
buys nothing but a working-tree switch nobody asked for, at the very end of a
session that is about to end anyway.

Measured across the four captured sessions, all of which ran the canon step
verbatim: in `295e2230` (2026-07-26) the auto-mode classifier **denied**
`git checkout main` twice — once inside a `fetch && checkout && pull` chain
(08:26:09→08:26:39, 30s) and once alone (08:27:13→08:27:40, 27s) — 57s of dead
wall time plus three recovery calls, after which the session read the capture
script's header and concluded the checkout had never been needed. The bare
`git fetch origin main` in between succeeded on the first try. The same step
cost 44s in `13a6f736` and 8s in `558026a0` for no benefit either. Leave the
tree on the merged branch and fetch.

**The fetch is denied sometimes too — one retry, then move on.** The permission
classifier is non-deterministic and not scoped to the checkout: the bare
`git fetch origin main` has been denied outright, and an identical immediate retry
has both failed and succeeded. Each denial costs 30–45s, and nothing downstream
needs the fetch — a run that was denied twice ran `capture-log.mjs` anyway and the
capture landed. So: one retry, and a denial is never an error to report, escalate,
or work around. Decomposing the command or switching tools to get the same bytes
spends the session's last minutes on a sync that buys nothing.

1 # gcec rules 2 3 The project's standing working rules — injected at session start while this pack 4 is declared. Activity-scoped procedures live in this pack's skills 5 (snapshot-approval, merge-and-ci, testing-guide) and surface on 6 demand; the extractor-automation domain's standing rules are the "Extractor 7 pipeline" section below, and its scheduled tasks live under `tasks/`. 8 9 ## Working rules 10 11 - **Never carry uncommitted edits onto a new branch with 12 `git checkout -- `** — that restores the paths' *committed* 13 content, silently destroying exactly the edits it was meant to preserve. 14 `git checkout -b origin/main` already brings a clean working tree along; 15 when it can't, commit or `git stash` first and never in the same `&&` chain 16 that moves the branch. In #734 the combined one-liner wiped three finished 17 edits **and** invalidated the `check_the_world.mjs` + `npm run test:offline` 18 pass that had just gone green, forcing a full re-verification. 19 - **A duplicate dispatch-trigger arriving while a session's own delegated 20 subagent is still running is a signal to stop, not to investigate.** 21 Confirm it via `resolve-dispatch` (the "not mine, change nothing" case) and 22 end the turn — don't let that check snowball into re-reading the subagent's 23 targets and redoing its work. In #876 a dispatched `tidy-issues` subagent 24 was still running in the background when a duplicate webhook fired; the 25 top-level session's "just confirming" pass over all 16 target issues 26 escalated into closing one and posting reconfirmation comments on the 27 rest — duplicating, not verifying, work its own subagent was already 28 producing — and converged the dispatch issue on that duplicate instead of 29 the subagent's actual output. 30 - **Cap and qualify every GitHub MCP list/search call** — an unbounded one 31 hard-fails the tool-result cap and costs a 2–3-call dig through the saved 32 result file. `search_issues` handed a bare title string full-text-searches the 33 whole repo and returns every match with its full body: the standing 34 `Claudinite tracker: ` lookup that opens every scheduled task blew up at 35 185–211 KB three times (#734 twice, #753), and `actions_list` without a page 36 cap at 155 KB (#760). Qualify the query (`in:title "Claudinite tracker: 37 "`, or `list_issues` + `labels`) **and** pass a small `perPage` (5–10) — 38 the answer wanted is one issue or one run, never a page of them. `perPage` 39 alone isn't the whole fix: even a single matched issue's full body can be 40 100+ KB, so the same overflow recurred with `in:title` correctly set but 41 `perPage` left off (#879, #890, #896). Pass `fields` too (e.g. `['number', 42 'title', 'state']`) to strip the body outright — a query that added it 43 (#886) returned instantly at ~3 KB where the identical unfielded query the 44 day before (#879) overflowed at 113 KB. 45 - **This repo's one divergence from the canon merge recipe: CI must be green 46 first** — twice for e2e/heavy-browser changes. The project mechanics of driving 47 a merge (dispatching CI in a web session, the poll back-off, when to arm 48 auto-merge instead of waiting) are the merge-and-ci skill — **load it for any PR a session opens**, including one 49 opened incidentally mid-task by an unattended run, not only for a deliberate 50 merge. 51 - **`npm run regen` is the regenerator** (load lists + UI snapshots + 52 generic-coverage baseline/report); a stale artifact can't slip through — its 53 own gate fails. On the `ours` driver (kept in sync with `.gitattributes`): 54 `extension/event-extractors/load-order.generated.json` (from `npm run index`), 55 `dev/requirements//cases/*.png` (from `npm run refresh:ui`), and 56 `dev/requirements/extractor/generic-coverage/generic-coverage.baseline.GENERATED.json` 57 + `generic-coverage.GENERATED.md` (from the generic-coverage test). The 58 inline gallery in `dev/requirements/requirements.md` is part-authored prose — 59 **not** on the `ours` driver; reconcile via `npm run regen` + the gallery 60 drift gate. If `regen` reports a coverage regression, that's the real gate 61 firing — review it, don't paper over it. 62 - **Keep divergence small**: when syncing a branch to `origin/main` (by rebase), 63 **run `npm run regen`** as part of the sync, so the branch carries 64 freshly-generated artifacts, not just the latest sources. 65 66 ## Owner commands 67 68 - **"bump version"** = cut a release **end to end** — bump, merge, and wait for 69 the published artifact. The bump mechanics are the canon `bump-version` 70 skill's; honor an explicit target ("bump version to 1.4.0") or level ("bump 71 patch" / "bump major") when given. Open the PR, 72 get CI green, squash-merge with `(#N)` — 73 saying "bump version" is itself the merge authorization for **this** 74 deterministic bump PR only. The merge triggers **Release: Create Package**; 75 do **not** report done until the `vX.Y.Z` GitHub Release with its refreshed 76 `google-calendar-event-creator.zip` asset is published — poll via the GitHub 77 MCP tools on the merge-and-ci skill's back-off. 78 - **"learned lessons"** = run the canon lessons-learned pass over the current 79 conversation on **the strongest model available**.
